newsitem.title: GERMANY: Economists see no change in German interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Economists see no change in German interest rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank will leave interest rates on autopilot at its council meeting on Thursday as economists said inflation was tame and the strengthening mark should not be provoked.

All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters said the German central bank would keep rates on hold. Only one economist predicted a cut in the discount and Lombard rates this year while none predicted a rate rise during the rest of 1997.
The survey showed economists expect the discount rate, the floor on German rates, to remain at 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate, the ceiling, at 4.50 percent.
The main money market rate, the securities repurchase rate, or repo, was expected to be kept at a fixed 3.00 percent.
"The economy is showing signs of recovery and a strengthening of the mark should not be provoked, so there is no reason to cut interest rates," said Mathias Haffner, an economist at BZW in Frankfurt.
"We have weak domestic demand and no danger of inflation at the moment so there is no reason to put rates up," he said.

The Federal Statistics Office underscored the tame inflation outlook, saying on Tuesday that Germany's consumer price index was unchanged in April compared to the previous month and registered a gain of just 1.4 percent year-on-year.
The statistics office said the consumer price index for the country as a whole stood at 117.9 in April, the same level as for March.
For west Germany, price pressures were even less in evidence, with April consumer prices falling 0.2 percent in April compared with March and rising 1.3 percent year-on-year.
East German prices continued to rise in April, up 0.2 percent month-on-month and 1.5 percent year-on-year.

"There is no need for the Bundesbank to move in either direction at the moment. The economy is fine and there is no danger of overheating. We will not see an increase in interest rates for the next 12 to 15 months," said Armin Kayser, senior economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt.
The weaker dollar, which fell to 1.70 marks this week from a 37-month high in April near 1.73 marks, would also prompt steady rates.
Some economists have said the Bundesbank had no reason to be alarmed at the dollar's recent strength.

But the currency market limits the chance for a rate cut even though recent economic data and comments from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan have allayed market fears that U.S. interest rates were poised to rise sharply this year.

"Key Bundesbankers have indicated lately that German monetary policy is set to remain the same, and the recent appreciation in the deutschemark reinforces that," said Craig Shute, economist at Bear Stearns in London.
